concept.body: A coordinate proof with VARIABLES covers every figure of its kind at once. Strategy: place a vertex at the origin, run a side along an axis, and use symmetry (isosceles → (±a, 0), (0, b)) — rigid motions guarantee nothing is lost. Varignon's theorem: the four side midpoints of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram, because each midpoint segment is a midsegment parallel to a diagonal at half its length.

check.body: One instance of the general fact.
explanationVariants: The midsegment copies the diagonal at half length: 12/2 = 6.

widget.prompt: A quadrilateral's diagonal measures 12. The two midpoint-figure sides parallel to it each measure ?

commonErrors.feedback: 12 is the diagonal itself — midsegments run at HALF: 6.

steps.body: Numbers prove ONE figure; **variables prove them all**. Place a general rectangle at (0, 0), (a, 0), (a, b), (0, b) — chapter 1's “cheap placement” advice paying off — and both diagonals compute to √(a² + b²). No specific rectangle was harmed: the congruent-diagonals theorem is proved for every rectangle at once.

explanationVariants: Diagonal 1: (0,0) to (a,b) — √(a² + b²). Diagonal 2: (a,0) to (0,b) — √((−a)² + b²), the same.

widget.prompt: Rectangle (0,0), (8,0), (8,6), (0,6) — the general proof's a = 8, b = 6 instance. Both diagonals measure ?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 = 8 + 6 walks the legs — the diagonal cuts across: √(64 + 36) = 10.
100 is the SQUARED diagonal — take the root: 10.
48 = 8 × 6 is the AREA — the diagonal is √(8² + 6²) = 10.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √(8² + 6²) = 10, twice — as the variables promised for every a, b.

steps.body: Placement is strategy. Put a vertex at the origin; run a side along an axis; exploit symmetry (an isosceles triangle as (−a, 0), (a, 0), (0, b) makes the equal slants √(a² + b²) automatic). Good placement costs nothing — rigid motions from the transformations course guarantee the figure is the same — and buys zeros everywhere.

explanationVariants: Midpoints: (4,1), (9,5), (6,7), (1,3). Opposite slope pairs: (5−1)/(9−4) = 4/5 twice, and (7−5)/(6−9) = −2/3 twice.
Both midpoint-quad slope pairs match: parallelogram — from a fully IRREGULAR quadrilateral.

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral (0,0), (8,2), (10,8), (2,6) — the figure's own. Join the four side midpoints in order. Compute the slope of the side joining midpoints (4, 1) and (9, 5).

commonErrors.feedback: 1.25 = 5/4 inverts — rise over run is (5 − 1)/(9 − 4) = 4/5 = 0.8, and the OPPOSITE midpoint side matches it.
−0.67 ≈ −2/3 belongs to the OTHER pair of midpoint sides — this one climbs at 4/5 = 0.8.
4 is the rise alone — divide by the run 5: 0.8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: (5 − 1)/(9 − 4) = 4/5 — and its opposite partner (1,3)→(6,7) matches: Varignon's parallelogram.

explanationVariants: Each midpoint side joins midpoints of two triangle sides — the midsegment: parallel to the third side (a DIAGONAL) at half its length.
Both members of a pair copy the SAME diagonal — so they're parallel to each other. Every quadrilateral, no exceptions.

widget.prompt: The figure shows each midpoint-parallelogram side parallel to a diagonal. Why does that prove Varignon for EVERY quadrilateral?

options.label: Each midpoint segment is a triangle midsegment over a diagonal — both segments of a pair copy the same diagonal, so they're parallel to each other
options.feedback: Split the quadrilateral along a diagonal: two triangles, two midsegments, one shared direction — the figure's color pairing IS the proof.

options.label: Because the example quadrilateral was special
options.feedback: The example was deliberately irregular — the midsegment argument uses no special property, so it covers all quadrilaterals.

options.label: Because midpoints always form squares
options.feedback: Squares only appear for special parents — the guaranteed outcome is a PARALLELOGRAM, via the shared-diagonal midsegments.

options.label: It only works for convex quadrilaterals
options.feedback: The midsegment argument never uses convexity — even crossed quadrilaterals obey it.

widget.prompt: To prove a theorem about a general ISOSCELES triangle by coordinates, the strongest placement is:

choices.label: (−a, 0), (a, 0), (0, b) — the axis of symmetry becomes the y-axis and the equal slants are automatic
choices.feedback: Symmetric placement makes both slants √(a² + b²) by construction — the isosceles hypothesis is encoded, not assumed mid-proof.

choices.label: (0, 0), (a, 0), (b, c) with all different letters
choices.feedback: Legal but leaky — three free letters encode a GENERAL triangle, and the isosceles condition returns as an equation you must drag along. Symmetry is cheaper.

choices.label: (1, 1), (5, 3), (3, 7) — nice concrete numbers
choices.feedback: Concrete numbers prove ONE triangle — the general claim needs variables.

choices.label: Placement doesn't matter at all
choices.feedback: Correctness survives any placement, but EFFORT doesn't — rigid motions (tm) license the cheap seat, so take it.

widget.successFeedback: Symmetric placement makes both slants √(a² + b²) by construction — the isosceles hypothesis is encoded, not assumed mid-proof.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open at least two coordinate-proof states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Inspect the coordinate invariants, then choose the supported conclusion.

widget.prompt: In the Varignon figure the diagonal from (0,0) to (10,8) has length √164. Each midpoint side parallel to it has length √41. Compute √164 / √41.

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the RATIO OF SQUARES (164/41) — lengths take the root: 2. The midsegment is HALF the diagonal.
0.5 inverts — the diagonal is the LONGER one: √164/√41 = 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √164/√41 = √4 = 2 — midsegments run at half the diagonal, the second half of Varignon.

hints: Varignon on a RECTANGLE: the parent's diagonals are congruent (proved in k1).
The midpoint parallelogram's sides are HALF the diagonals — all four sides equal half of √(a²+b²).
A parallelogram with four equal sides has a name from pq.
explanationVariants: All four midpoint sides measure ½√(a² + b²) — equal — so the midpoint figure is a RHOMBUS, for every rectangle. (With a = 8, b = 6: four sides of 5.)
Congruent parent diagonals ⇒ equal midsegments ⇒ rhombus. Instance check: ½(10) = 5 four times.

widget.prompt: Take the rectangle (0,0), (8,0), (8,6), (0,6) and join its side midpoints. Every side of the resulting figure measures ?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 is the parent DIAGONAL — each midpoint side is a midsegment at HALF that: 5 (four times: a rhombus).
7 = (8 + 6)/2 averages the rectangle's sides — the midsegments copy half the DIAGONAL √100: 5.
25 is the squared side — the length is 5, four times over: the midpoint rhombus.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each side = ½√(8² + 6²) = 5 — four equal sides: the rectangle's midpoint figure is always a rhombus.

takeaways: General placement (origin + axes + symmetry) turns one computation into a theorem for every figure.
Varignon: side midpoints of ANY quadrilateral form a parallelogram — midsegments copy the diagonals at half length.
Special parents pass traits down: congruent diagonals (rectangle) ⇒ midpoint rhombus.
